facts.claim: UNESCO page title is 'Albanian folk iso-polyphony'; inscribed in 2008 (3.COM) on the Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity, originally proclaimed in 2005.

UNESCO: the music 'traditionally accompanies a wide range of social events, such as weddings, funerals, harvest feasts, religious celebrations and festivals', including the folk festival in Gjirokastra. UNESCO also tags the element 'Wedding'.

UNESCO: two major stylistic groups, the Ghegs of northern Albania and the Tosks and Labs of the south; the 'iso' is a drone accompanying polyphonic singing; rendered mainly by male singers; today transmitted mainly through professional folk artists rather than within the family.

The Australian Embassy, Rome covers Italy, San Marino, Albania and Libya and provides consular assistance to Australians in Albania; its consular page links notarial services, marriage overseas and apostilles.

Smartraveller Albania (updated 16 October 2026, current 3 November 2026): Australia has no embassy or consulate in Albania; consular help comes from the Australian Embassy, Rome. Overall level 'Exercise a high degree of caution' due to limited healthcare options; no higher-level areas.
Smartraveller Albania: same-sex relationships are legal but not widely accepted; avoid public displays of affection. The page says nothing about same-sex marriage.
Smartraveller Albania: a person born in Albania or with an Albanian parent is an Albanian national; male dual nationals may face military service.

Smartraveller Albania: limited medical facilities, especially outside Tirana; insurance must cover medical evacuation. Extreme temperatures and forest fires April to October. Regular political protests; avoid large gatherings.

Smartraveller 'Getting married overseas' (updated 18/08/2026): some countries ask you to prove you aren't already married; each country decides what proof it accepts; most common are a Certificate of No Impediment to Marriage (CNI) or registry certificates (no-record statement, Single Status certificate, No Record Result certificate). Local authorities may also ask for divorce papers, a deceased spouse's death certificate, original birth certificate and passport. Some countries have residency rules. 'We can't tell you what you will need'; contact the destination's embassy or consulate.

Smartraveller CNI page (updated 01/10/2026): DFAT issues CNIs through Australian Passport Offices, Australian embassies and consulates overseas, and by mail; at least one applicant must be an Australian citizen or permanent resident; some authorities only accept a CNI issued in their country; ask whether the CNI needs an apostille or authentication certificate; documents not in English need a professional English translation; sign the form only before an authorised witness.
DFAT charges a fee for a CNI and for an apostille (fee schedule from 1 January 2026, indexed to CPI each 1 January). A fee applies; amounts deliberately not carried into the article (no-prices rule).
facts.conflicts: Amounts are published on the page; per brief no prices are used. Flagged to Nic in needs_signoff in case any amount is ever quoted.

facts.claim: Smartraveller: you can't register an overseas marriage in Australia, but in most cases it is legally recognised if valid where it happened and valid under Australian law had it occurred here. A foreign marriage certificate is usually accepted as proof but may not work as proof of a name change. Not recognised where a party is already married, under age, too closely related or forced. Talk to a lawyer to confirm validity.

SEARCH-SUMMARY-ONLY (not opened; non-official, not a primary source): a National Albanian Registry article snippet (albanianregistry.org, 5 June 2026) calls the krushqeria 'the groom's procession to the bride's home to fetch her'; other search snippets (blogs, shops) describe the krushqit as wedding guests from the groom's side who travel to collect the bride. Use only to support 'often told' wording, never as a fact.

insider_details.detail: There is no Australian embassy in Albania, so any CNI, apostille or consular step runs through the Australian Embassy in Rome or a Passport Office in Australia; sort documents before flying.

Ask the Albanian civil status office early whether it accepts a CNI issued in Australia, and whether it must carry an apostille, because some authorities only accept locally issued CNIs and Australia has no mission in Albania to issue one there.

Iso-polyphonic singing is a genuine wedding-linked tradition on UNESCO's own page; it is mainly sung by men and now passed on through professional folk artists, so couples who want it will be booking a performing group rather than relying on family.

Outdoor celebrations between April and October sit in Smartraveller's extreme heat and forest fire window; build shade, a heat plan and guest travel insurance with medical evacuation into summer weddings, especially outside Tirana.
Albanian-Australian guests or partners may be Albanian nationals by birth or parentage, and male dual nationals may face military service, so they should read Smartraveller before travelling.
